# Part 1 · Our Pine Needles — Start With Data You Trust

::: callout-important
## Column names in `pine_data.csv` / `pine_data.xlsx`

Both files hold the **same six columns, with exactly these names**. Type them
exactly as written — R is case-sensitive, and `Needle_Length` or `needle_length`
will not work:

| Column             | What it is                                     |
|--------------------|------------------------------------------------|
| `source_file`      | the raw team file the row came from             |
| `team`             | field team — one team = **one tree**            |
| `replicate`        | needle number within a tree side (1-8)          |
| `side`             | sun exposure — `"shady"` or `"sunny"`           |
| `needle_length_mm` | needle length, millimetres                      |
| `needle_width_mm`  | needle width, millimetres                       |

After you read the file in, click `pine_df` in the **Variables** pane in Positron
and check the names against this table before you write any other code.
:::

Last week you ran a paired t-test on our four trees and got **p = 0.072**. Before we reach for anything non-parametric, we have to establish that we actually *need* it — so we start by checking the assumptions on the data you collected yourselves.

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 1.1 · Setup and our pine needles ─────────────────────────────
library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)     # round_half_up(), used inside summary_stats()
library(car)         # leveneTest()
library(patchwork)   # combining plots
library(perm)        # permutation tests
library(effectsize)  # cohens_d()

source("themes_functions/r_themes_and_functions.R")

pine_df <- read_csv("data/pine_data.csv")

# same two-stage summary as the t-test lecture
p_df <- pine_df %>%
  group_by(team, side) %>%
  summarise(needle_length_mm = mean(needle_length_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop")

p_wide_df <- p_df %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = side, values_from = needle_length_mm)

p_wide_df
```

**▶ Run this — do the assumptions actually hold?**

``` r
# ── Part 1.2 · Checking the assumptions first ─────────────────────────
# normality, one side at a time -- all 32 needles per side
shapiro.test(pine_df$needle_length_mm[pine_df$side == "sunny"])
shapiro.test(pine_df$needle_length_mm[pine_df$side == "shady"])

# equal variance
leveneTest(needle_length_mm ~ factor(side), data = pine_df)
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Record the three p-values, and remember which way these tests point — **H₀ is that the assumption holds.**

```         
Shapiro-Wilk, sunny:   p = ______
Shapiro-Wilk, shady:   p = ______
Levene's test:         p = ______
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Based on those three numbers, is there any assumption of the paired t-test you ran last week that you can reject?

`________________________`

✏️ **Your turn:** So — do these data *need* a non-parametric test?

`________________________`

## Effect size — a demonstration

::: callout-note
**👀 Read this one, don't sweat it**

This section is here so you have *seen* effect size before we need it in the power lecture. Run the two blocks, read the output, answer the two short questions. There is nothing to get stuck on.
:::

Your paired t-test last week gave **p = 0.072** — "not significant." But `p` never said *how much* shorter the shady needles were. **Cohen's d** does: it is the difference between groups measured in standard deviations, so it carries no units and can be compared across studies.

For a paired design, `d` is the mean of the paired differences divided by the standard deviation of those differences.

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 1.3 · Effect size (demonstration) ────────────────────────────
diffs <- p_wide_df$shady - p_wide_df$sunny

mean(diffs) / sd(diffs)     # Cohen's d, by hand

# and with a confidence interval
cohens_d(p_wide_df$shady, p_wide_df$sunny, paired = TRUE)
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Write the value of `d` and its confidence interval here, then say in one plain sentence what the `d` value means.

```         
d  = ______        95% CI = [ ______ , ______ ]

In words: the shady side averaged ______ standard deviations
          ____________ the sunny side.
```

**▶ Run this — why it matters:**

``` r
# ── Part 1.4 · Effect size (demonstration) ────────────────────────────
2.7227 / sqrt(4)      # our paired t statistic, divided by the square root of n
```

Compare that number to your `d`. They are the same, because **t = d × √n** — the t-statistic is the effect size multiplied by the square root of your sample size.

✏️ **Your turn:** If a p-value depends on **both** the size of the effect **and** how many samples you took, why is reporting `d` alongside `p` more informative than reporting `p` on its own?

`________________________`

::: callout-important
**⚠️ The sentence worth remembering**

"No significant difference" sounds like *we found nothing*. Our four trees actually gave a **large** effect (d = −1.36) that we simply could not pin down (the CI runs from −2.74 to 0.10). Those are very different messages, and only the second one is honest.
:::

Now back to the rank tests. Run them even though the assumptions held — the point of this part is to find out what that choice would have cost you.

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 1.5 · The two rank-based tests ───────────────────────────────
# unpaired: Mann-Whitney U
wilcox.test(needle_length_mm ~ side, data = p_df)

# paired: Wilcoxon signed-rank
wilcox.test(p_wide_df$shady, p_wide_df$sunny, paired = TRUE)
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Fill in the comparison table.

```

unpaired:               p = 0.425         p = ______
paired:                 p = 0.072         p = ______
```

# Part 2 · A Dataset Where the Assumptions Really Do Fail

Part 1 showed you what non-parametric tests **cost**. It could not show you what they **buy** you, because nothing about the pine data was broken.

The lake trout data is a genuine mess: six lakes, wildly unequal sample sizes, and mass distributions that fail every check we just ran. Everything from here on uses `mass_g`.

Let's start by exploring only lake NE 12, as if doing a single-sample t-test, then compare NE 12 to Island Lake.

We want to test if the mass of lake trout in NE 12 differs from a mean of 500g.

# Part 3 · Testing Assumptions on NE 12

Before conducting our t-test, we need to verify our data meets the necessary assumptions. Methods to test normality: visual (QQ plots, histograms) and statistical (Shapiro-Wilk test).

**▶ Run this** — histogram:

``` r
# ── Part 3.1 · Testing Assumptions on NE 12 ─────────────────────────────
ne12_histo_plot <- ggplot(ne12_df, aes(x = mass_g)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 200) +
  labs(x = "mass (g)", y = "Frequency")
ne12_histo_plot
```

**▶ Run this** — dotplot, boxplot, and QQ plot:

``` r
# ── Part 3.2 · Testing Assumptions on NE 12 ─────────────────────────────
ne12_dot_plot <- ggplot(ne12_df, aes(x = mass_g, y = "")) +
  geom_dotplot(binwidth = 60, stackdir = "center", fill = "darkblue", dotsize = 0.5) +
  labs(title = "Dotplot", x = "Mass (g)", y = "")
ne12_dot_plot

ne12_box_plot <- ggplot(ne12_df, aes(y = mass_g)) +
  geom_boxplot(fill = "darkblue") +
  labs(y = "Mass (g)", x = "") +
  coord_flip()
ne12_box_plot

ne12_qq_plot <- ggplot(ne12_df, aes(sample = mass_g)) +
  stat_qq(color = "darkblue") +
  stat_qq_line() +
  labs(title = "QQ Plot", x = "Theoretical Quantiles", y = "Sample Quantiles") +
  theme_regular(base_size = 10) +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5))
ne12_qq_plot
```

**▶ Run this** — combine all four with patchwork:

``` r
# ── Part 3.3 · Testing Assumptions on NE 12 ─────────────────────────────
combined_stats_plot <- (ne12_histo_plot + ne12_dot_plot) / (ne12_box_plot + ne12_qq_plot) +
  plot_annotation(
    theme = theme(plot.title = element_text(hjust = 0.5),
                  plot.subtitle = element_text(hjust = 0.5))
  )
combined_stats_plot
```

**▶ Run this** — the formal test (note: really you want to do this on residuals, but here we test the raw values directly):

``` r
# ── Part 3.4 · Testing Assumptions on NE 12 ─────────────────────────────
shapiro_test <- shapiro.test(ne12_df$mass_g)
shapiro_test
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Does the QQ plot agree with the Shapiro-Wilk result? Is NE 12's mass normally distributed?

# Part 4 · Comparing Two Lakes — NE 12 vs. Island Lake

Now that we've shown NE 12's mass fails (or passes) normality, let's explore a comparison of NE 12 and Island Lake `mass_g`.

**▶ Run this** — build the two-lake data frame:

``` r
# ── Part 4.1 · Comparing Two Lakes ──────────────────────────────────────
in_df <- lt_df %>%
  filter(lake %in% c("NE 12", "Island Lake")) %>%
  filter(!is.na(mass_g))
head(in_df)
```

**▶ Run this** — summary stats by lake:

``` r
# ── Part 4.2 · Comparing Two Lakes ──────────────────────────────────────
summary_by_lake <- in_df %>% group_by(lake) %>% reframe(summary_stats(mass_g))

summary_by_lake
```

**▶ Run this** — histograms by lake:

``` r
# ── Part 4.3 · Comparing Two Lakes ──────────────────────────────────────
hist_plot <- in_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = mass_g, fill = lake)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(x = "Mass (g)", y = "Count") +
  theme_regular(base_size = 10) +
  facet_wrap(~lake, scales = "free_y")
hist_plot
```

**▶ Run this** — QQ plots by lake (in a QQ plot, points that follow the line indicate normally distributed data; deviations suggest non-normality):

``` r
# ── Part 4.4 · Comparing Two Lakes ──────────────────────────────────────
qq_plot <- in_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(sample = mass_g, color = lake)) +
  stat_qq() +
  stat_qq_line() +
  labs(title = "QQ Plot for Normality Check",
       x = "Theoretical Quantiles", y = "Sample Quantiles") +
  theme_regular(base_size = 10) +
  facet_wrap(~lake)
qq_plot
```

**▶ Run this** — the formal test, done for each lake separately (note: Island Lake can look non-normal in the QQ plot but come out close to normal in the Shapiro-Wilk test):

``` r
# ── Part 4.5 · Comparing Two Lakes ──────────────────────────────────────
normality_results <- in_df %>%
  group_by(lake) %>%
  summarize(
    shapiro_stat = shapiro.test(mass_g)$statistic,
    shapiro_p_value = shapiro.test(mass_g)$p.value,
    normal_distribution = if_else(shapiro_p_value > 0.05, "Normal", "Non-normal")
  )
normality_results
```

**▶ Run this** — Levene's test for equal variances (H₀: variances are equal across groups; we want this **non-significant**):

``` r
# ── Part 4.6 · Comparing Two Lakes ──────────────────────────────────────
levene_result <- leveneTest(mass_g ~ lake, data = in_df)
levene_result
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Based on your normality and Levene's test results, do these two lakes meet the assumptions for a standard t-test?

# Part 5 · Data Transformations

A log₁₀ transformation commonly helps right-skewed data like this pass the normality assumption.

**▶ Run this:**

``` r
# ── Part 5.1 · Data Transformations ─────────────────────────────────────
in_df <- in_df %>%
  mutate(log_mass = log10(mass_g))
head(in_df)
```

**▶ Run this** — check if it worked, with a histogram:

``` r
# ── Part 5.2 · Data Transformations ─────────────────────────────────────
log_hist_plot <- in_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = log_mass, fill = lake)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 20, alpha = 0.7) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Log-Transformed Lake Trout Mass",
       x = "Log10 Mass", y = "Count") +
  theme_regular(base_size = 10) +
  facet_wrap(~lake, scales = "free_y")
log_hist_plot
```

**▶ Run this** — a QQ plot of the transformed data (we'll skip Shapiro-Wilk for a moment):

``` r
# ── Part 5.3 · Data Transformations ─────────────────────────────────────
log_qq_plot <- in_df %>%
  ggplot(aes(sample = log_mass, color = lake)) +
  stat_qq() +
  stat_qq_line() +
  labs(title = "QQ Plot for Log-Transformed Data",
       x = "Theoretical Quantiles", y = "Sample Quantiles") +
  theme_regular(base_size = 10) +
  facet_wrap(~lake)
log_qq_plot
```

**▶ Run this** — now the formal tests on the transformed data:

``` r
# ── Part 5.4 · Data Transformations ─────────────────────────────────────
log_normality_results <- in_df %>%
  group_by(lake) %>%
  summarize(
    shapiro_stat = shapiro.test(log10(mass_g))$statistic,
    shapiro_p_value = shapiro.test(log10(mass_g))$p.value,
    normal_distribution = if_else(shapiro_p_value > 0.05, "Normal", "Non-normal")
  )
log_normality_results

levene_log_result <- leveneTest(log_mass ~ lake, data = in_df)
levene_log_result
```

✏️ **Your turn:** Did the log transformation fix normality, equal variance, both, or neither?

# Part 6 · Running the Tests

Even if the transformation doesn't fully fix things, let's run the full set of tests so we can compare them side by side.

**▶ Run this** — standard two-sample t-test on the raw data:

``` r
# ── Part 6.1 · Running the Tests ────────────────────────────────────────
t_test_result <- t.test(
  mass_g ~ lake,
  data = in_df,
  var.equal = TRUE,
  alternative = "two.sided"
)
t_test_result
```

**▶ Run this** — the same t-test on the log-transformed data:

``` r
# ── Part 6.2 · Running the Tests ────────────────────────────────────────
log_t_test_result <- t.test(
  log_mass ~ lake,
  data = in_df,
  var.equal = TRUE,
  alternative = "two.sided"
)
log_t_test_result
```

::: callout-note
**When analyzing log-transformed data:**

1.  The mean of log-transformed data, back-transformed, gives the *geometric mean* (not the arithmetic mean).
2.  The back-transformed confidence intervals represent the CI for the geometric mean, and must be calculated carefully.
3.  Report results like: "The geometric mean mass of lake trout in NE 12 was X g (95% CI: Y–Z)."
4.  You can't just take `10^SE` to get the standard error — instead, back-transform `mean - se` and `mean + se` separately.
:::

**▶ Run this** — back-transform to the geometric mean:

``` r
# ── Part 6.3 · Running the Tests ────────────────────────────────────────
back_transformed <- in_df %>%
  group_by(lake) %>%
  summarise(
    n = n(),
    mean_log = mean(log_mass),
    sd_log = sd(log_mass),
    se_log = sd_log / sqrt(n),
    geometric_mean = 10^mean_log,
    lower_se = 10^(mean_log - se_log),
    upper_se = 10^(mean_log + se_log),
    arithmetic_mean = mean(mass_g)
  )

back_transformed %>%
  select(lake, mean_log, geometric_mean, arithmetic_mean)
```

**▶ Run this** — plot the back-transformed geometric means (note the error bars are not symmetrical!):

``` r
# ── Part 6.4 · Running the Tests ────────────────────────────────────────
geo_mean_plot <- back_transformed %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = lake, y = geometric_mean, fill = lake)) +
  geom_bar(stat = "identity", width = 0.5, alpha = 0.7) +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = lower_se, ymax = upper_se), width = 0.2, linewidth = 1) +
  labs(title = "Geometric Mean Lake Trout Mass with Standard Error",
       subtitle = "Back-transformed from log10 scale",
       x = "Lake", y = "Geometric Mean Mass (g)") +
  theme_regular(base_size = 10) +
  theme(legend.position = "none")
geo_mean_plot
```

**▶ Run this** — Welch's t-test (doesn't assume equal variances):

``` r
# ── Part 6.5 · Running the Tests ────────────────────────────────────────
welch_test_result <- t.test(
  mass_g ~ lake,
  data = in_df,
  var.equal = FALSE,
  alternative = "two.sided"
)
welch_test_result
```

> 💡 Welch's t-test is preferred when group variances are unequal (per Levene's test), sample sizes differ between groups, or you just want a more robust default.

**▶ Run this** — the Mann-Whitney Wilcoxon test (non-parametric):

``` r
# ── Part 6.6 · Running the Tests ────────────────────────────────────────
wilcox_test_result <- wilcox.test(
  mass_g ~ lake,
  data = in_df,
  alternative = "two.sided"
)
wilcox_test_result
```

> 💡 Mann-Whitney is preferred when data isn't normal even after transformation, you're comparing medians rather than means, or outliers might distort a t-test — it compares ranks, not raw values.

**▶ Run this** — a permutation test (balance the sample sizes first):

``` r
# ── Part 6.7 · Running the Tests ────────────────────────────────────────
set.seed(123)  # For reproducibility

island_size <- sum(in_df$lake == "Island Lake")

ne12_sample <- in_df %>%
  filter(lake == "NE 12") %>%
  slice_sample(n = island_size)

balanced_df <- bind_rows(
  ne12_sample,
  in_df %>% filter(lake == "Island Lake")
)

perm_test_result <- permTS(
  mass_g ~ lake,
  data = balanced_df,
  alternative = "two.sided",
  method = "exact.mc",
  control = permControl(nmc = 10000)
)
perm_test_result
```

> 💡 Permutation tests are useful for small samples, data that doesn't meet parametric assumptions, or when you want a test that makes minimal distributional assumptions — and they can test statistics other than the mean.

::: callout-tip
**🚀 If you finish early:** Rerun the permutation test with `nmc = 1000` instead of `10000`. Does the p-value change meaningfully? What's the tradeoff of using fewer Monte Carlo replications?

# Part 7 · Comparing All Results

**▶ Run this** — build a comparison table:

``` r
# ── Part 7.1 · Comparing All Results ────────────────────────────────────
test_results <- data.frame(
  Test = c("Standard t-test",
           "Log-transformed t-test",
           "Welch's t-test",
           "Mann-Whitney Wilcoxon test"),
  Statistic = c(paste("t =", round(t_test_result$statistic, 2)),
               paste("t =", round(log_t_test_result$statistic, 2)),
               paste("t =", round(welch_test_result$statistic, 2)),
               paste("W =", wilcox_test_result$statistic)),
  p_value = c(t_test_result$p.value,
             log_t_test_result$p.value,
             welch_test_result$p.value,
             wilcox_test_result$p.value),
  Significant = c(t_test_result$p.value < 0.05,
                 log_t_test_result$p.value < 0.05,
                 welch_test_result$p.value < 0.05,
                 wilcox_test_result$p.value < 0.05)
)
test_results
```

When reporting results, include:

- **Standard t-test:** "Lake trout from NE 12 had significantly different mass (M = \[mean\], SD = \[SD\]) compared to Island Lake (M = \[mean\], SD = \[SD\]), t(\[df\]) = \[t-value\], p = \[p-value\]."
- **Log-transformed t-test:** "After log transformation to meet normality assumptions, lake trout from NE 12 had significantly different mass (geometric mean = \[value\], 95% CI \[lower–upper\]) compared to Island Lake (geometric mean = \[value\], 95% CI \[lower–upper\]), t(\[df\]) = \[t-value\], p = \[p-value\]."
- **Welch's t-test:** "Assuming unequal variances, lake trout from NE 12 had significantly different mass (M = \[mean\], SD = \[SD\]) compared to Island Lake (M = \[mean\], SD = \[SD\]), Welch's t(\[df\]) = \[t-value\], p = \[p-value\]."
- **Mann-Whitney Wilcoxon test:** "Lake trout mass differed significantly between NE 12 (Mdn = \[median\]) and Island Lake (Mdn = \[median\]), W = \[W-value\], p = \[p-value\]."
- **Permutation test:** "Permutation testing (10,000 iterations) revealed significant differences in lake trout mass between NE 12 and Island Lake, p = \[p-value\]."

This time the test itself is the question. You now know five ways to compare two groups — standard t-test, log-transformed t-test, Welch's t-test, Mann-Whitney, and permutation test. Given a new dataset, you decide which one is appropriate and defend your choice.

## Background

Male sagebrush crickets (*Cyphoderris strepitans*) have an unusual mating system: during copulation the female eats the tips of the male's hind wings and drinks his haemolymph. A male who has already mated has damaged wings, and is therefore visibly "starved" relative to a virgin male.

The question is whether that costs him. Johnson et al. measured **time to mating** — how many hours a male waited before securing a mate — for males that had already mated (**starved**) and males that had not (**fed**).

::: callout-important
**⚠️ This is Example 13.5 in Whitlock & Schluter**

These are the data the textbook uses to introduce the Mann-Whitney U test in **Chapter 13**. That is deliberate: after you have made your own decision and written it up, you can read the chapter and see how the authors justified theirs.

**Do the work first.** The point of this assignment is your reasoning, not matching the book.
:::

::: callout-important
## Column names in `sage_brush_crickets_feeding_mating.csv`

| Column | What it is |
|--------------------|------------------------------------------|
| `feeding_status` | `"fed"` (virgin male) or `"starved"` (already mated) |
| `time_to_mating_h` | hours the male waited before mating |
:::

# Conclusion

Two datasets, two different answers to the same question — *which test does this data deserve?*

On the **pine needles** the assumptions held, and the rank-based tests cost us power for nothing. On the **lake trout** the assumptions failed badly, and those same tests were exactly the right tool. Non-parametric is not a safe default; it is a response to a specific problem.

When assumptions *are* violated:

1.  Try transforming the data (e.g., log transformation)
2.  Use Welch's t-test if variances are unequal
3.  Use non-parametric tests (Mann-Whitney or permutation tests) if data remains non-normal

All methods have strengths and limitations, and consistency of results across methods can strengthen your conclusions.

::: callout-note
**When to use each test**

- **Standard t-test:** data is normally distributed with equal variances
- **Log-transformed t-test:** raw data is skewed but log-transformation achieves normality
- **Welch's t-test:** variances are unequal
- **Mann-Whitney Wilcoxon test:** data is not normal and cannot be transformed to normality
- **Permutation test:** sample sizes are small, or assumptions cannot be met
:::
